summary: Presents use cases from diverse industries that need deterministic flows, meaning guaranteed bandwidth, bounded latency, and similar properties for time-sensitive data. They differ in topology and behavior and give context for Deterministic Networking (DetNet). It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of real jobs, like factory machines and power grids, where data must arrive on time without fail, to show why special networks are needed.

subtitle: Nine industries that need network data to arrive on time, every time, and what they ask of the IETF.

tldr.problem: Many industries, from pro audio to power grids, need flows with guaranteed bandwidth and bounded latency, but today they rely on proprietary networks or on Layer 2 LANs whose flows cannot be routed over IP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes use cases in nine areas. For each it says what the use case is, how it is handled today, how it should be handled in future, and what the IETF should deliver, then pulls out common themes.
tldr.outcome: It gives context for Deterministic Networking (DetNet) design decisions and acts as a yardstick for judging designs. It does not specify any DetNet architecture or protocol.

facts.value: 250 us max in the LTE example; 100 us in one specification

today: RFC 8578 is an Informational document and the data lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records use cases and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: What the Use Cases Are For
sections.content:
This memo documents use cases for industries that need deterministic flows over multi-hop paths: flows with guaranteed bandwidth, bounded latency and other properties for time-sensitive data. DetNet flows can start from a Layer 2 or Layer 3 interface, can coexist with best-effort traffic, and can use redundant paths for high reliability.

The use cases were originally not considered concrete requirements. The DetNet Working Group and Design Team judged which elements fit the DetNet charter, and moved the rest to Appendix A. The document gives context for design decisions, helps newcomers, and has served as a yardstick for proposed designs. It explicitly does not suggest any specific architecture or protocol, and DetNet does not itself handle clock distribution or time synchronization.

The industries are professional audio and video, electrical utilities, building automation, wireless for industrial applications, cellular radio, industrial machine to machine, mining, private blockchain, and network slicing.
sections.plainLanguage: Before building a special road for ambulances, you first list who needs to get places fast and why. This document is that list.

sections.title: Pro Audio and Video
sections.content:
Professional audio and video (music and film creation, broadcast, cinema, live sound, venue systems) is moving from point-to-point links to packet networks. Deterministic flows exist today inside standards-based Layer 2 LANs such as IEEE 802.1 TSN, but those flows are not routable via IP, and ProAV has no way to build them from a standards-based Layer 3 interface.

Live playback cannot be fixed by retrying, since a retry comes too late. Audio and video must stay in sync within about one NTSC video frame (about 33 ms), and a sound-reinforcement system becomes unusable if delay exceeds about 10-15 ms for the whole signal path. Where audio phase matters, latency can be in the 10 us range.

The RFC also wants reserved bandwidth that is unused to be available to best-effort traffic, redundant paths, traffic segregation for cheap sink devices, and a single network for A/V and IT traffic. As an example, a broadcast studio had to join its Layer 2 islands with a custom SDN router because no standards-based routing solution existed.
sections.plainLanguage: If the sound reaches your ears a moment after the picture, a movie feels wrong. These systems need the sound and picture to travel at steady speeds across big buildings.

sections.title: Electrical Utilities
sections.content:
Utilities depend on networks for transmission, generation and distribution. The most demanding case is teleprotection: communication links and protection relays isolate faults on high-voltage lines and equipment. Power-line equipment can tolerate a fault for about five power cycles, a total clearance time of 100 ms. Protection systems are limited to 70-80% of that, and some switches leave only a 10 ms window for telecommunications. IEC 61850-5:2013 limits transfer time for the most critical messages to 4-8 ms for 60 Hz lines.

Differential schemes need matching transmit and receive delays; legacy relays tolerate discrepancies of up to 750 us. Tables in the RFC give network metrics for each scheme, such as one-way maximum delay, 99.9999% availability, redundancy, and recovery on node failure in less than 50 ms with no packet loss visible (hitless).

The RFC also discusses generation and distribution, migration from legacy TDM to packet networks, Precision Time Protocol use and security practices in utility networks.
sections.plainLanguage: When a power line breaks, a warning must reach the switch in a few thousandths of a second so it turns off before anything is damaged. A late warning is as bad as none.

sections.title: Buildings, Factories, Radios and More
sections.content:
Building automation: a BAS measures device states, stores and reports data, raises alarms and controls devices such as HVAC. The ask is a converged, interoperable network with delays from under 10 ms to 100 ms in a network of several hundred devices, jitter under 1 ms and availability up to 99.9999%.

Wireless industrial: the focus is 6TiSCH (IPv6 over the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping mode of IEEE 802.15.4e), a wireless technology that provides deterministic QoS; other deterministic wireless networks are incompatible with each other and with IP.

Cellular radio: fronthaul links base stations to remote radio heads. In an LTE example, of 3 ms for processing a radio frame, the fronthaul gets a maximum one-way delay of 250 us, and one specification allows only 100 us, roughly 20 km of optical fiber. Fronthaul today is typically dedicated fiber with proprietary protocols.

Industrial M2M: PLCs on a plant floor exchange periodic control streams, served today by proprietary networks. Mining uses remote control of autonomous trucks and vehicles and wireless monitoring. Private blockchain runs on managed networks that today carry its traffic best-effort. Network slicing splits one physical network into logical networks, and DetNet could give hard isolation between slices.
sections.plainLanguage: Smart buildings, factory robots, phone towers, mines and shared networks each need their messages to arrive on time. Today each has its own special wiring, and they would like one shared kind.

sections.title: Common Themes
sections.content:
Section 11 sums up what the use cases imply. A DetNet network is not a new kind of network: it is based on extensions to Ethernet standards such as IEEE 802.1 TSN, is expected to be centrally administered rather than plug and play, and should integrate Layer 2 and Layer 3. It is meant as an open alternative to proprietary deterministic networks, and to let time-sensitive and IT traffic share a network.

  • Packets in a DetNet flow are guaranteed not to be dropped due to congestion, though not against media or checksum errors.
  • Unused reserved bandwidth is available to best-effort traffic moment to moment, but not to other time-sensitive traffic, which needs its own reservation.
  • Networks should allow bounded latency, low latency, bounded jitter and symmetrical path delays, and should say so if a requested service level is unavailable.
  • Availability may need to reach 99.9999% or even 12 nines, using redundant paths to switch seamlessly.
  • Reserved flows must be isolated from each other and from best-effort traffic. DetNet scope excludes unbounded decentralized networks such as the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: All these jobs want the same few things: messages that never get stuck in traffic, always arrive in the same amount of time, and have a backup road if one breaks.

sections.title: Security and Out-of-Scope Cases
sections.content:
Each use case has its own security concerns, from use-specific and DetNet technology perspectives. For a fuller discussion the RFC points to a separate DetNet security considerations document. It notes that time-sensitive data must arrive at the expected time as well as with the intended content, which may be a new security challenge. The document has no IANA actions.

Appendix A lists use cases moved out of scope, including Internet-based applications such as media content delivery, online gaming and virtual reality, and some pro audio topics such as digital rights management and link aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: Being on time is part of being safe: a correct message that arrives too late can still cause trouble. The detailed safety rules live in another document.
